extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Persian theatre, comparative literature, cultural history, and performance studies
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive-analytic guidance and evaluative observations about Persian tazya (Passion plays) focusing on staging, performance practices, audience rituals, language, and religious reception. Useful for analyzing or reconstructing these performances historically or for creative adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: These pieces are given in the first ten days of the month of Moharrem, the anniversary of the martyrdom at Kerbela.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The season (Moharrem) is central to meaning and reception; although popular pieces may 'invade other seasons' they are most powerful and ubiquitous during these solemn first ten days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity and social reach
rubrics_metrics.description: They are so popular that they invade other seasons of the year; 'King and people, every one is in mourning' and representations can bring together thousands (even 20,000 at Ispahan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure significance by cross-class attendance, patronage (from king to beggar), and the scope of public participation; popularity explains scale of material resources and civic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processional and communal mourning rituals
rubrics_metrics.description: Processions keep passing, the air resounds with the beating of breasts and with litanies of 'O Hassan! Hussein!' Confraternities go in procession with a black flag and torches, every man with his shirt torn open, and beating himself with the right hand on the left shoulder in a kind of measured cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance is embedded in broader public ritual: chanting, litanies, and bodily displays are part of the dramatic event and essential to its effect on audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical, visceral displays (self-mortification and spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies of dancers strike wooden castanets and Berbers carry iron chains and long needles, move violently and 'begin to beat themselves with their chains and to prick their arms and cheeks with the needles — first gently, then with more vehemence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violent, physical elements (self-flagellation, piercing) intensify pathos and recall ancient sacrifice; include such elements only with awareness of cultural and ritual meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, funding, and patronage of tekyas
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatres (tekyas) are constantly multiplying; the king, great functionaries, towns, wealthy citizens or any private person provide them. There are tekyas for a few hundred up to representations bringing twenty thousand people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource availability determines size and elaboration; contributions are treated as religious offerings, so social obligation and patronage shape construction and ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tekya spatial arrangement and stage architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The tekya is a walled parallelogram with a brick platform (sakou) in the centre; a reserved box (tdgnumd) higher than the sakou is used for magnificent tableaux; passages and surrounding boxes, tiers of seats and a stretched awning with masts characterize the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct or evaluate staging by noting central sakou as performance space, the elevated tdgnumd for tableaux, audience tiers, and protective awning and masts as fixed elements that determine blocking and sightlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience proximity and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The foremost rows sit on their heels close up to the passage so that they help the actors to mount and descend when they pass between the sakou and the tdgnumd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close physical proximity blurs barrier between actors and spectators; audience participation (helping actors, joining chants) is an intrinsic performance dimension rather than incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual opulence of setting and spectators
rubrics_metrics.description: A sea of colour and splendour: woodwork and brickwork disappear under cushions, rich carpets, silk hangings, embroidered muslin, shawls from Kerman and Cashmere, coloured lamps, mirrors, Bohemian and Venetian glass, porcelain vases, paintings and engravings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extravagant display and decorative richness contribute to the spectacle’s emotional effect even when scenic illusion is minimal; lavishness is a feature to be documented or preserved in adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal scenic contrivance and reliance on audience imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: In marked contrast with the display is the poverty of scenic contrivance and stage illusion. A copper basin represents the Euphrates; a heap of chopped straw is the sand of Kerbela; no attempt at proper costume; the imagination of the spectator fills up all gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plays rely on symbolic props and audience imaginative participation rather than realistic scenery; authenticity of effect comes from solemnity and communal imagination, not elaborate illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume approach (symbolic rather than historically accurate)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no attempt at proper costume; all that is sought is to do honour to the personages by dresses and jewels which would pass for rich and handsome things in modern Persian life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costume functions symbolically (signifying richness/honour) rather than as period-accurate reconstruction; emphasis is on recognizability and reverence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting style: emotional sincerity and identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors 'throw his whole soul into what he is about' and 'the actor identifies himself with the personage he represents to such a degree that...he cannot be said to act...he reaches a reality...and produces impressions...which it would be simply absurd to look for from our more artificial performances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power derives from genuine seriousness, enthusiasm, and self-forgetfulness; emotional authenticity is prized over technical artifice or stylized 'acting'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of actors and acceptance of open technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors are visible on all sides, and the exits, entrances, and stage-play of our theatres are impossible; the imagination of the spectator fills up all gaps and meets all requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arena-style, fully visible performance is normative; do not aim to hide theatrical mechanics—audiences accept and participate in the convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting conventions and role of children/boys
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors are men and boys, the parts of angels and women being filled by boys. The children who appear are often the children of principal families and 'do not consider themselves to be acting; they are full of the feeling that what they are about is something of deep seriousness and importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting follows social and ritual logics (boys for women/angels, notable families’ children for blessing); children’s earnest participation is a valued element that enhances pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language register and rhetorical differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic pieces are in popular language, free from learned Arabic words; 'The Imams and their families speak always in a kind of lyrical chant...their persecutors, the villains of the piece, speak always in prose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain popular diction accessible to the uninstructed; differentiate speakers by style—lyrical chant for sanctified figures and prose for antagonists—to signal moral/aesthetic stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious orthodoxy and clerical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Moollahs (regular ecclesiastical authorities) condemn the whole thing as an innovation 'addressed to the eye' and bringing in 'novelties and heresies'; learned critics call the pieces 'a heap of lies' produced by ignorant people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of doctrinal objections (visual representation of sacred matters, narrative accretions); evaluate or stage with sensitivity to orthodox critiques and the tension between popular devotion and learned disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and authority of the choragus (oosiad)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage is under the direction of a choragus called oosiad, 'a sacred personage' who sometimes addresses the audience, prays, preaches, remains constantly on stage with the book in his hand, gives actors their cue, dresses the martyr, and inserts supplies of chopped straw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central directing figure with evident ritual authority organizes the spectacle and mediates between performers and audience; this role combines stage direction, liturgical function, and practical stage management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical signals and spontaneous chants
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifes, drums, and trumpets break out; the kernas (great copper trumpets) give notice that the actors are ready; wild chants and litanies are set up by a dervish, a soldier, a workman and are taken up by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music serves both formal signaling and spontaneous communal expression; evaluate timing, instrumentation (kernas), and points where audience-led chanting may crescendo into paroxysm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic cycle structure and episode selection
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a clear notion of the cycle: begin with pieces relating to the childhood of the Imams (e.g., The Children Digging) and culminate in the tenth day with the death of the Imam himself; the cycle includes well-known items like The Marriage of Kassem and The Christian Damsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full cycle spans many episodes across days; programming choices (which episodes on which days) shape cumulative emotional effect and theological messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tableaux and magnificent set-pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The tdgnumd box is used for 'peculiarly interesting and magnificent tableaux' (e.g., the court of the Caliph); 'the crown jewels are lent for it' and dresses may be worth thousands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite minimal illusion elsewhere, staged tableaux and occasional richly staged set-pieces serve as focal visual moments; these require special resources and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritualized audience practices integrated into performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members perform commemorative acts (young men 'deal out water all round' in memory of thirst), the Family of the Tent put the Koran on their heads and pray covering themselves with sand, and the public beats its breast and cries 'Fa Allah! 0 God!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance and devotion are entwined: ritual gestures by the audience are part of the dramatic grammar and must be accounted for in any analysis or revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic props and simple representational devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Props serve symbolic functions (a copper basin = Euphrates; chopped straw = desert sand; empty water-bottle as 'a silent token of distress').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the evocative power of minimal props rather than literalism; small symbolic objects often carry strong emotional resonance within this tradition.
